title: Embryonic nicotine exposure causes major brain malformations in Xenopus

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Embryonic nicotine exposure causes major brain malformations in Xenopus

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Exposing Xenopus laevis embryos to nicotine (0.1 mg/mL, stages 10–35) causes major brain morphology defects (absent nostrils, forebrain or midbrain, misformed hindbrain) in about 55% of tadpoles at stage 45, compared with about 6% of controls.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Pai VP 2018, HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns › Results › Embryonic nicotine exposure induces brain morphology defects

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Nicotine exposure caused a significantly high incidence of major brain morphology defects (~55%) in comparison to controls (~6%).

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Pai VP, Pietak A, Willocq V, Ye B, Shi NQ, Levin M, “HCN2 Rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns”, Nature communications (2018), doi:10.1038/s41467-018-03334-5; section “Results › Embryonic nicotine exposure induces brain morphology defects”. Scope: Xenopus laevis embryos exposed to 0.1 mg/mL nicotine from stage 10 to 35, scored at stage 45

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2018-hcn2-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The exposure, endpoint, and effect size are direct and standard. Published group data support a substantial audit, but full independent confirmation depends on availability of individual embryo records and images.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Blindly score predefined major brain defects at stage 45 in nicotine-exposed and untreated embryos and estimate incidence with clutch-level uncertainty. Support requires the reported large treatment-control difference without differential mortality.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The extent of openly downloadable individual-level morphology data is unclear.

Clutch effects and scoring blinding need explicit handling.

fields.value:
data existence: 0.7
discriminating power: 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The defect classes, dose, stages, and approximate rates are explicit published measurements. They can be checked for a large treated-versus-control gap. Because the embryo-level scores and images are not openly deposited, the percentages cannot be recomputed or audited for scoring bias, which leaves the result partly resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Score stage-45 tadpoles for absent nostrils, forebrain, or midbrain and for misformed hindbrain after 0.1 mg/mL nicotine from stages 10 to 35, against untreated siblings. A major-defect rate near 55% versus near 6% in controls would support the result; overlapping rates would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The data-availability statement leaves raw scores with the corresponding author.

The published rates are approximate, and nicotine has several targets besides the brain-voltage pattern.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.45
data adequacy: 0.4
discriminating power: 0.5
operationalizability: 0.88
analysis feasibility: 0.42

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: In published embryo-level counts, Xenopus laevis embryos exposed to 0.1 mg/mL nicotine (stages 10-35) show major brain morphology defects at stage 45 at a much higher rate (about 55%) than untreated controls (about 6%).

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py downloads the Pai et al. 2018 full text and the Tung et al. 2024 Source Data, checks that the quoted incidence sentences and the figure-legend group sizes occur verbatim in the full text, and reconstructs counts as round(percentage x 153), 153 = 3 experiments x 51 embryos being the smallest total consistent with 'N > 50 embryos per treatment group for each of those experiments'. It runs a two-sided Fisher exact test for Fig. 1d (primary) and Fig. 5f (repeat within the paper) and reports the smallest per-group N at which p < 0.001 would still hold. Tung et al. per-replicate nicotine defect percentages by group size are summarized as context.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: from published counts (affected / scored tadpoles) for nicotine-exposed and control embryos under the claim's protocol, (a) the incidence of major brain defects is >= 40% with nicotine and <= 15% in controls, and (b) the difference is significant by a two-sided Fisher exact test at p < 0.001. If only percentages and group sizes are published, counts are reconstructed as round(percentage x n) and this is stated.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: nicotine incidence minus control incidence < 10 percentage points, or Fisher p >= 0.05. Outcomes in between (significant but outside the magnitude bands in (a)) are pre-registered as 'mixed'. If no counts or group sizes for both groups can be obtained from a public source, the verdict is 'inconclusive' (data-unavailable).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: percent of stage-45 tadpoles with major brain defects, nicotine vs control (Pai et al. 2018 Fig. 1d, as reported)

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: counts reconstructed at the legend's lower bound N = 153 per group; Fisher p = 3.62e-22

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'Major brain morphology defects' follows the paper's scoring (absent nostrils, forebrain or midbrain, or misformed hindbrain at stage 45). The test checks that the published counts support the stated incidence contrast; with only the source paper's data available it is an audit of the reported numbers, not an independent replication, and is labelled as such. Mortality differences, clutch structure and blinding cannot be assessed from aggregate counts. The claim's mechanistic context (nicotine acting through disruption of the brain bioelectric prepattern) is not tested.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Pai et al. 2018, HCN2 rescues brain defects by enforcing endogenous voltage pre-patterns, Nat Commun 9:998 (full text XML, PMC5843655)

Tung et al. 2024, Embryos assist morphogenesis of others through calcium and ATP signaling mechanisms in collective teratogen resistance, Nat Commun, Source Data file

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Not independent: the only admissible counts are the source paper's own, and only as rounded percentages ('~55%', '~6%') with a lower bound on group size. The test confirms that the reported numbers, taken at face value, meet the pre-registered contrast with a wide margin (p < 0.001 would hold with as few as 21 embryos per group); it cannot check scoring, blinding or mortality.

Fisher's test treats embryos as independent. The paper's own analysis used n = 3 experiments (t-test, p < 0.01), and clutch effects could make the embryo-level p far too small; the effect size (about nine-fold) is the more robust quantity.

Within the paper the contrast repeats (Fig. 5f: ~60% vs ~7%), but that is the same lab and protocol.

Context from a later Levin-lab study (Tung et al. 2024, same dose, stages 11-35): the nicotine-induced brain-defect rate depends strongly on how many embryos are reared together, from 96.7% in groups of 10 to 46.9% at 50, 22% at 100 and 10.1% at 125. Nicotine reliably causes brain malformations, but 'about 55%' is a property of the rearing conditions, not a fixed teratogenic rate. Those values are normalized to untreated controls and so do not test the 6% control rate.

Pai et al. state that individual-level data are available from the corresponding author on request; no embryo-level table is deposited, and the supplementary PDF contains only model notes.
